title: Comparing Sparsified MLPs and Transcoders: Many Transcoder Features Are Neurons in Disguise
authors: Stepan Shabalin, Mateusz Piotrowski
abstract: MLP neurons in transformer language models are widely understood to be polysemantic, motivating transcoders - sparse, learned approximations of MLP layers - as interpretable replacement models for mechanistic analysis. However, recent work shows that MLP neurons can be used to recover sparse, interpretable circuits (Arora et al. 2026, Ye et al. 2025), raising the question of whether transcoders are necessary for circuit analysis. title: How Well Can LLMs Verbalize Mathematical Formulas? A Multi-Domain Evaluation
authors: Peter Volbach, Tim Schlippe
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across natural language tasks. But their ability to generate accurate written verbalizations of mathematical formulas has not been systematically evaluated. Such verbalization is important for text-to-speech systems supporting audio-based learning and visually impaired users. title: MisleadQA: Diagnosing LLM Failures under Misleading Context
authors: Hui Wang, Bohao Chu, Qianli Wang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer questions from retrieved or user-provided context. However, provided context can be factually true yet out-of-scope, describing a different entity, time, or location from the one the question targets, and still lead models to a wrong answer. title: CADS: Measuring the Incremental Contribution of LLM Proposers in Sequential Biological Screens
authors: Guanxing Chen, Nihui Shao, Haohuai He et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to guide sequential biological screens, yet standard evaluations rely on raw hit counts that conflate a proposer's value with the discovery capacity of the underlying algorithmic harness. Adaptive sampling and corrupted experimental readouts also leave standard feedback comparisons without a false-discovery guarantee. title: WAQS: Weight Absorption for Quadratic Probing and Affine Steering
authors: Ding Zhu, Mohammad Mahdi Khalili
abstract: Activation steering provides a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for controlling large language model behavior. Existing methods, however, often face a trade-off between efficiency and expressiveness: fixed steering vectors incur negligible inference overhead but cannot adapt to the current model input, whereas input-dependent nonlinear interventions provide greater flexibility at additional runtime cost. title: FlashMap: Flow Map Speculative Decoding
authors: Jeff Shen, Zhejian Zhou, Ryan Lee et al.
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass. Autoregressive drafters generate this block one token at a time, whereas block diffusion drafters such as DFlash generate it in one pass, making drafting faster. title: What Matters for NVFP4 Training? A Comparative Study of Low-Precision Pretraining Recipes
authors: Anjulie Agrusa, Andrei Panferov, Elizabeth Wei et al.
abstract: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating-point (FP) formats promises substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency. While some recipe design choices have been validated at scale, many promising approaches remain untested beyond small models and short token horizons, leaving open the question of which trends will hold. title: fxBench: Evaluating and Understanding Formula Suggestions in Spreadsheets
authors: Sanket Mhatre, Sumit Gulwani, Vu Le et al.
abstract: Spreadsheets are among the most widely used tools for computations, and formulas are their core building blocks. Besides agentic spreadsheet tools, proactive formula suggestions enable significant productivity gains and are now available in popular spreadsheet software (Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets). title: PV-Decoding: Progressive Verification Decoding with Decode Gating for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Renxi Liu, Yiming Li, Shengyin Sun et al.
abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an attractive alternative to autoregressive generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, but their inference efficiency is still limited by the cost of safely committing tentative predictions. title: Write Once, Query Many: Evolving Compact Reusable Memory for Long Videos
authors: Kerui Chen, Jinglu Wang, Yun Wang et al.
abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. title: Which Long Documents Matter? A Controlled Study of Data Selection for Context Extension
authors: Junlong Jia, Jiang Zhou, Xing Wu et al.
abstract: Natural long documents are widely used for context extension, but which selection pipelines are effective remains unclear. We conduct a controlled comparison on Qwen2.5-3B at 128K under matched 6B-token continued-training budgets. Random sampling of natural long documents (random-long) outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths. title: Long Listening Thoughts: Eliciting Open Auditory Reasoning with Deliberative Perception and Cognitive Refinement
authors: Jaeyeon Kim, Chao-Han Huck Yang, Luoyi Zhang et al.
abstract: We introduce Long Listening Thoughts (LLT), a framework for constructing post-training datasets that improves audio reasoning by pairing deliberate perceptual grounding with explicit cognitive behaviors. On audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, large audio-language models (LALMs) are limited primarily by perceptual errors, yet existing post-training datasets rely on audio descriptions of limited diversity. title: Blackbox Performance Analysis of LLM-based Network Control
authors: Mahdi Alizadeh, Pooria Namyar, Arvin Ghavidel et al.
abstract: LLMs are becoming an indispensable part of network control systems due to their impressive reasoning. Before such LLM-enabled systems can be deployed, it is imperative to develop tools that can audit their performance on previously unseen inputs. However, auditing these systems is challenging due to the inherent opacity of LLMs. LENS is the first step towards black-box performance analysis of LLM-enabled network control systems. title: GRaSP: Latency-Aware Optimization for Geo-Distributed Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Hardik Ruparel, Raj Kumar Pandey, Pramod Kumar
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is increasingly served across geo-distributed cloud and edge infrastructures, where wide-area latency, cross-region egress cost, and data-residency rules compete with retrieval quality. Conventional pipelines rank by semantic similarity alone and ignore where content lives, inflating tail latency and cost. title: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
authors: Zachary Cutts, John Coller, Rachel Chen et al.
abstract: Despite breakthroughs in AI-driven molecular generation, existing discovery pipelines operate largely in silico, with wet-lab feedback reserved for validation rather than iterative improvement. Whether large language model (LLM)-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with lab data remains unproven. title: AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
authors: Bohan Yu, Pengfei Cao, Kai Tian et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) possess broad factual knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, but solving complex tasks also requires procedural knowledge about how to act. Existing approaches often represent procedural knowledge through trajectories or bundled skills, limiting flexible reuse across interaction histories. title: MedPAO-Assist: Edge-Deployable, Modality-Aware Agentic AI for Radiology Report Structuring
authors: Shrish Shrinath Vaidya, Minmini Selvam, Ganapathy Krishnamurthi
abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models for radiology report structuring has been largely dominated by either proprietary cloud-based models or large open models requiring high-end GPUs for deployment, which is a critical bottleneck for clinical adoption in radiology workflows that demand data privacy and offline operation. title: Enhancing RAG-based Medical VQA with Gated Multimodal Representations
authors: Daniela Jimenez-Pano, Hugo Jair Escalante, Delia Irazú Hernández-Farías
abstract: Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) have shown strong performance in Medical Visual Question Answering (MVQA), yet they may still produce factually inconsistent responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can mitigate this issue by incorporating external clinical evidence; however, retrieval is often guided by a single modality, potentially overlooking the joint semantics of medical images and clinical questions. title: Characterising and Analysing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Techniques
authors: Emmanuel Igbekele, Olawande Daramola
abstract: The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) across many application domains has increased the need for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM performance. Thus far, several RAG techniques with impressive features and capabilities have been proposed in the literature, making it a herculean task to select the most appropriate RAG techniques for specific problem scenarios. title: On the Position Bias of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Study
authors: Yining Li, Huayang Li, Lemao Liu et al.
abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. title: AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery
authors: Shicheng Liu, Krista Opsahl-Ong, Andrew Drozdov et al.
abstract: Reproducible and analytically robust research findings are essential to scientific progress, but evaluating these properties typically requires costly manual effort. We investigate whether LLM agents can help automate reproduction and robustness analysis, using a medical case study grounded in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, a widely used U.S. cancer registry underlying tens of thousands of published studies. title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
authors: Jiaming Xu, Hanzhen Wang, Tianlang Zhao et al.
abstract: Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. However, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. title: On the possibilities and limitations of LLM-based multi-agent systems for multi-criteria decision-making in healthcare operations management
authors: Marco Boresta, Tommaso Giovannelli, Sepehr Namirad et al.
abstract: Multi-criteria models for healthcare operations need weights that express how stakeholders trade off patient waiting time, provider workload, and operating cost, but these weights are difficult to quantify. Teams of large language model (LLM) agents, each prompted to represent a stakeholder, have been used to supply them. title: From Trajectories to Differentiated Skills: Cognitive Differentiation for Self-Improving Agents
authors: Yewei Zhao, Derong Xu, Wei Chen et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents tackle complex tasks through reasoning and interaction with external environments. Agent skills provide persistent, transferable capabilities that guide task planning, inform contextual decisions, support tool use, and enable executable procedures. title: RL-Guided Temporal Localization for Dual-Channel Retrieval in Long-Horizon Agent Memory
authors: Dabin Sheng, Zhe Wu, Jinming Zhao et al.
abstract: Time-aware retrieval is crucial for long-horizon LLM agents to effectively leverage ever-growing long-term memory. Existing methods focus on lexical or semantic similarity, leading to target memories being crowded out by temporally mismatched yet semantically similar candidates. title: Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents
authors: Mingze Yin, Xiaohan Wang, Dian Li et al.
abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across complex tasks, they predominantly operate in isolated sessions, lacking the ability to continually learn from historical interactions or adapt to user-specific environments. Existing self-evolution paradigms often indiscriminately inject raw interaction trajectories into memory or skill modules, leading to obscured behavioral patterns and compromised update controllability. title: SkillBrowser: Selective Skill Exposure for Scalable Skill-Using Agents
authors: Jin Ye, Yifan Jiang, Lan-zhe Guo
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on skills to extend their capabilities in complex tasks. However, scalable skill use requires Selective Skill Exposure (SSE): providing relevant procedural content when needed while avoiding unnecessary exposure that may disrupt reasoning. Existing paradigms fall short in complementary ways. title: Robust Function Calling for LLM Agents Under Interface Drift
authors: Aniruddha Chattopadhyay, Kanishka Halder, Partha Sarathi Roy
abstract: Tool-augmented language-model agents rely on interface text: tool descriptions, argument schemas, and the candidate tool list shown at inference time. These interfaces often change after deployment even when the underlying tool semantics remain fixed, creating a practical reliability problem for function-calling systems. title: AgentOnto: Ontology-Guided LLM Agents for Enterprise Data Analytics
authors: Dayan Pan, Bincheng Zuo, Xiaojian Wang et al.
abstract: Enterprise data analysis requires agents to connect analytical requests with knowledge distributed across databases, business documents, and existing example tasks. Without an explicit representation of this knowledge, an agent may produce incorrect analytical results and cannot reliably incorporate feedback. title: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection
authors: Songping Wang, Peiyang Li, Yi Huang et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based mobile agents are rapidly evolving from conversational assistants into autonomous systems that perceive, reason over, and act on smartphone environments. This capability also exposes a new security risk: adversaries can embed malicious objectives in cross-application mobile content and steer agent behavior through indirect multimodal injection. title: Annotrace: A Workbench for Step-Level Annotation of Agent Traces
authors: Arun Josephraj Arokiaraj, Chenyi Huang, Sahan Bulathwela et al.
abstract: Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. title: Beyond Marginal Influence: Interaction-Aware Memory Selection for LLM Agents
authors: BHVSP Subrahmanyam, Neeraj Choudhary
abstract: LLM-agent memory selection often uses retrieval rankings based on record relevance or individual influence. Such rankings cannot identify sufficient subsets under redundant or jointly necessary evidence. We study per-decision memory sufficiency: selecting a small subset that preserves full-memory behavior. title: MAS-Bai: Linguistically Informed Adaptive Multi-Agent Translation for Bowen-Script Bai
authors: Jingting Zheng, Hong Ren, Yuehan Cui et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain unreliable for extremely low-resource languages whose writing systems conflict with high-resource pretraining priors. We study Bai-Chinese translation in the Bowen script, where Chinese characters are frequently borrowed phonetically rather than semantically, causing severe literal-translation hallucinations. title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Heming Zou, Qi Wang, Yixiu Mao et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. title: Disentangling Language Effects on Tool Admission and Post-Retrieval Safety
authors: Aditya Nawal, Manit Baser, Mohan Gurusamy
abstract: LLM agents increasingly use retrieval tools across languages, yet their safety evaluation remains English-centric. It remains unclear whether language affects tool admission, post-retrieval generation, or both. authors: Aditya Nawal, Manit Baser, Mohan Gurusamy
abstract: Large language models increasingly act as agents that call external tools, yet most tool-safety research examines only what follows a tool call. The prior decision of whether to call the tool remains largely unexamined and can influence downstream safety. Across the seven open-weight models, the unweighted model-average harm rate after admitted harmful requests is 74.5%. title: ParetoChat: An LLM-Based Interface for Interactive Multi-Objective Optimization
authors: Gokhan Ceyhan
abstract: Multi-objective optimization models are often deployed in settings where decision makers (DMs) must balance some conflicting criteria. In practice, however, stakeholders must translate their qualitative preferences between different criteria into numerical weights, priorities, or reference points required by optimization methods, which can be difficult to specify and interpret. title: Agentic In-Context Learning: What Algorithms Can Transformers Learn in Closed-Loop Interaction?
authors: Shiguang Wu, Yaqing Wang, Quanming Yao
abstract: The learning algorithm view of in-context learning (ICL) studies how fixed-parameter Transformers learn from supplied examples. Language model agents extend this setting through interaction: their actions determine what evidence enters context next. We call this regime Agentic In-Context Learning (Agentic ICL). title: Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them
authors: Weixiang Zhao, Yichen Zhang, Yanyan Zhao et al.
abstract: Experience-driven self-evolution offers a promising path for large language model (LLM) agents to continually improve through interaction. Yet existing approaches often rely on successful trajectories or external evaluation signals, leaving unclear whether agents can evolve when such positive anchors are unavailable. title: KiranaBench: Can a Language Model Run a Neighbourhood Shop?
authors: Bhuvan Arora, Ankita Karmakar, Chaitanya Jain et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on long-horizon tasks, including autonomously running a business. Existing benchmarks for this setting are almost exclusively English-language, Western in retail context, and single-agent, with the agent observing the business directly. We study how these results transfer to a multi-agent Indic setting. title: SAFE-Mem: Secure Agentic Memory with Fine-Grained Authority and Governance-Aware Retrieval
authors: Haoming Li, Dingyi Kang, Xu Hu et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent memory to support long-term reasoning and personalized interactions. However, information collected from external sources can introduce security risks when untrusted claims (i.e., atomic statements) are later treated as authorized preferences, policies, or permissions. title: Cooperation Without Adaptation: LLM Agents in a Collective-Risk Dilemma
authors: Trung-Kiet Huynh, Dao-Sy Duy-Minh, Chi-Nguyen Tran et al.
abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of people in settings where individual decisions shape shared outcomes. We examine whether five production models adapt their contributions to changing risks and partner behaviour, or instead follow a relatively fixed strategy. authors: Bowen Ding, Qixin Wang, Lexing Ruan et al.
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly integrated into real-world works, yet they must handle diverse domain-specific tools and complex multi-sub-task problems that sequential tool invocation resolves inefficiently and with severe context bloat. authors: Zhepei Wei, Wenlin Yao, Baolin Peng et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promising potential in coding tasks, and their performance is jointly determined by the policy model and the harness that mediates their interaction with the environment. title: When Can You Trust an Agent's Own Verifier? Stress-Testing Counterfactual Rationale Verification Under Search Pressure and Oracle Access
authors: Jonghyun Lee, Moonsu Kim, Sunghwan Park
abstract: Automated agent design increasingly trusts a single score to decide whether a change is an improvement -- but a score optimized aggressively enough ceases to measure what it was meant to. When an agent also explains its design, that explanation is a second signal we can check without human labels: negate each stated claim, re-run, and observe whether performance drops. authors: Yitian Zheng, Zhaorun Chen, Haoyu Li et al.
abstract: AI agents have increasingly interacted with external environments by invoking tools, with Model Context Protocol (MCP) emerging as a standard interface for connecting agents to heterogeneous tools and services. As organizations deploy agents at scale, MCP gateways have become a critical middleware layer for aggregating, governing, and shaping the tool surface exposed to agents. title: Beyond Large Language Models: A Mental World Model Framework for Mental Modeling, Simulation, Evolution, and Interpretability
authors: Qingshi Wang
abstract: Understanding and simulating how subjective cognition and mental states emerge, evolve, and shape behavior is essential for advancing artificial intelligence toward deeper social cognition and general intelligence. Existing large language models (LLMs) and Theory of Mind (ToM) methods primarily infer mental states from linguistic information, lacking unified mechanisms for subjective world construction, cognitive-psychological interactions, dynamic evolution, and historical dependencies. title: OwlSight: A Panoramic Monitor for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
authors: Lewen Yan, Yanxu Zhu, Jie Zhang et al.
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring offers actionable evidence for oversight AI systems, with the potential to enable early detection and intervention. However, existing approaches are focused on specific tasks, whereas the regulation of AI, particularly reasoning models, requires monitoring a broader range of tasks. title: Trapped in Your Story: Evaluating Narrative-Induced Sycophancy in Large Language Models
authors: Runtai Yang, Dandan Zhu, Kaiwei Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to exhibit sycophancy by adjusting their responses toward users' expressed views. However, real users often justify their opinions through reasons, personal experiences, causal explanations, and broader narratives, raising the question of whether such narratives can further steer model judgments. authors: Xin Qiu, Junlong Tong, Wei Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now perceive, describe, and reason about images and audio, yet time series understanding remains underestimated: most work uses LLMs as forecasters and classifiers, reasoning studies are few and narrow, and no suite trains and evaluates the full range of capabilities. authors: Wenda Li, Tongya Zheng, Shunyu Liu et al.
abstract: Graph Large Language Models (GraphLLMs) enable powerful semantic understanding and reasoning over Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs), while their semantic reasoning may exhibit vulnerabilities to perturbations in node text and graph structure under adversarial attack evaluation. authors: Jaewon Sok, Jewon Yeom, Seonghyeon Park et al.
abstract: Large language models often answer factual questions incorrectly in closed-book settings, and such errors are usually attributed to missing knowledge. Yet models often encode answers they fail to produce. We show that many closed-book errors are first-token recall failures: the model commits to a wrong first token, but once given the right one it completes the answer and often recognizes it as correct. title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs
authors: Fabian Broszio, Michael Hoffmann, Adrian Paschke
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent outputs that lack source support or conflict with local operational constraints. We introduce Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT), a modular architecture that organizes generation as a closed Retrieve--Reflect--Revise loop. authors: Yujing Wang, Yulan He, Wenya Wang et al.
abstract: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification methods detect reasoning faithfulness from model outputs or static activations, but are limited in explaining how unfaithfulness develops during generation. authors: Uriel Dolev, Idan Schwartz, Yoav Goldberg
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) controllability, the ability of reasoning models to control properties of their CoT, is consequential for both their usefulness and reliable oversight. title: Who Pays for Efficient Inference? Confidence-Based Small-to-Large LLM Routing Across Tasks and Languages
authors: Md Sabbir Hossen, Anichur Rahman, Pabon Shaha et al.
abstract: Small-to-large language model routing can reduce inference cost by escalating difficult inputs while retaining easier ones on a smaller model. Its success, however, depends on identifying examples that benefit from escalation, and the reliability of confidence across multilingual tasks remains unclear. authors: Ming Shen, Tianjun Yao
abstract: Test-time scaling methods implicitly assume that additional computation from the same model provides independent evidence. title: Prism Attention: Proposal-Refined Index Sharing Mechanism for Efficient LLMs Inference
authors: Zhenxu Tian, Kebin Liu, Zhengwu Yang et al.
abstract: Long-context decoding in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory and computation required to attend over an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache at each autoregressive step. title: Sep-Latent: Separator Tokens as Natural Compression Anchors for Implicit Reasoning
authors: Yinlong Xu, Jianfeng Huang, Zhengdong Zhou et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in complex reasoning through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the associated computational overhead and token verbosity remain significant barriers to efficiency. While implicit reasoning in continuous latent spaces offers a promising alternative, existing methods like Coconut and CODI often rely on fixed-length latent sequences and suffer from representational collapse. title: Competence-Based Evaluation of Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
authors: Jize Jiang, Chengxiang Zhai
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. title: NLData2Opt: Benchmarking Parameter Derivation and Prediction for Modeling Optimization Problems from Natural Language and Data
authors: Lijia Liu, Kyohei Atarashi, Jiyi Li et al.
abstract: Formulating optimization problems from raw inputs of problem descriptions and data is time-consuming and costly. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising way to automate this process, existing benchmarks overestimate their capabilities by relying on idealized inputs where all data is relevant and complete. title: Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Tree Search
authors: Jianguo Huang, Zhiyi Lyu, Fuxiang Zhang et al.
abstract: Tree search enhances multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet prevailing methods expand every step with a fixed budget, irrespective of the marginal utility of expansion. We first show, across existing search algorithms, that continuations sampled from a shared intermediate state are largely duplicates and collapse to a few distinct answers. title: The Reliance Hypothesis: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Rises as Language Resource Level Falls
authors: Lucas Resck, Jingyi Sun, Qianli Wang et al.
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness matters for monitoring, explaining and safely deploying large language models, yet it has been studied mostly in English. Languages differ in level, the amount of text available to learn from, so models know less in lower-resource languages, which may change how much they rely on their reasoning. title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models
authors: Oscar Kemme, Janek Haberer, Ali Hojjat et al.
abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. title: CoTA++: Understanding the Repeat Curse in dMLLMs from an Information Flow Perspective
authors: Qiyan Zhao, Xiaofeng Zhang, Xu-Yao Zhang et al.
abstract: Diffusion-based multimodal large language models (dMLLMs) decode by iterative denoising with bidirectional attention, which precludes the standard autoregressive key--value cache. Practical deployments therefore rely on approximate caching that reuses intermediate states across denoising steps. title: Causal Value Attribution of Marketing Labels in LLM-Generated Ads: A Deconfounder Approach
authors: Danhong You, Wei Jiang,  Zhiqiang et al.
abstract: As AI-generated content becomes commoditized, economic value increasingly shifts from final artifacts to the upstream expertise used to specify inputs that steer LLM generation. Yet organizations lack methods for valuing this expertise and identifying which individual skills or configurations causally improve performance. title: COMET: Decoupled Distillation, Routing, and Capacity Control for Task-Agnostic Continual Vision--Language Learning
authors: Seungyoon Woo, Keonhee Park, Gunhee Kim
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP retain zero-shot recognition ability, but their open-world use often requires task-agnostic continual learning: tasks arrive sequentially, past data are unavailable, task identity is unknown, and the backbone cannot be retrained. We argue that this setting fails VLMs through three coupled pressures beyond the stability-plasticity tradeoff: (1) modal-consistency drift, (2) representation-space interference, and (3) per-task capacity shortfall. title: FederatedBytes: Tokenizer-Free, Byte-Level Small Language Models for Efficient Multimodal Federated Learning
authors: Ali Sarabadani, Massimo Piccardi, Mehran Abolhasan et al.
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis. title: Beyond Reward Scoring: Online Multi-Agent Preference Learning for Multimodal Response Generation
authors: Ziyun Zou, Jiwoo Hong, Yifan Lu et al.
abstract: Multimodal preference alignment often follows a score-based RLHF pipeline: a reward model is first trained to learn human preferences, then used to score on-policy responses and optimize the response model's generation. title: VISTA: Steering LLMs with Latent User Values Inferred from a Few Survey Answers
authors: Yinuo Xu, Jadie Adams, Brian Hu et al.
abstract: Personalizing a language model requires knowing what a person values, which stays largely consistent across tasks. Yet most methods either learn task-specific preferences or place the user's profile in the prompt, where models struggle to act on it. title: Truth in Contrast: Calibrated Factual Evidence from Language Model Likelihoods
authors: Ponhvoan Srey, Jason Lucas, Pittawat Taveekitworachai et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge. Yet, estimating confidence in factual claims reliably remains challenging. We study likelihood-based factual confidence from the complementary perspectives of discrimination and calibration across multilingual factual statements. title: LocalIntent: Outcome-Specific Structured Generation for Backend-Compatible Smart Building Automation with Local LLMs
authors: Tianyang Liu, Jiayue Wang, Zhanhao Cheng et al.
abstract: Locally deployed large language models (LLMs) can reduce reliance on remote cloud services for natural language smart building automation, but backend-facing processing requires correct outcome selection, alignment with local capabilities, and valid structured outputs. title: ECHO: Replacing the Compliance Proxy with Response Harmfulness in Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attack
authors: Yuanwei Wu, Lingdong Huang, Yunlong Mao et al.
abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment, large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing optimization-based attacks share a single objective: maximize a token-level proxy of victim compliance---such as the likelihood of an affirmative prefix---computed on the prompt rather than the decoded reply. title: Controlling the Diversity-Quality Trade-Off of LLMs by Merging Models Before and After Alignment
authors: Yasuaki Sumita, Tomoharu Iwata, Toshiyuki Tanaka
abstract: Alignment is known to change the output characteristics of large language models (LLMs). Base models tend to generate more diverse outputs, whereas aligned models tend to produce higher-quality outputs. The appropriate balance between the two depends on the task. Existing methods either require costly fine-tuning or, like temperature sampling, mainly improve lexical diversity rather than semantic diversity. title: What Shapes Brain Alignment of Large Language Models during Dialogue? Insights from Language Production and Comprehension
authors: Yuko Nakagi, Yuya Chiba, Yasue Kishino
abstract: Brain alignment of large language models (LLMs) offers a way to investigate representational similarities between LLMs and the human brain during language processing. While previous studies have mainly focused on passive language comprehension, little is known about such alignment during dialogue, in which speakers engage in both language production and comprehension. In this study, using fMRI data collected during dialogue, we examine brain alignment during language production and comprehension

title: Aligning Language Models Towards Counterfactual Invariance
authors: Basar Demir, Emily Shen, Ksheeraj Sai Vepuri et al.
abstract: Small variations in prompt characteristics can meaningfully alter the semantics, tone, and contextual assumptions of large language model outputs. Such characteristics can involve group variables such as demographics or other sensitive latent attributes. title: Many Biases, One Circuit: Post-Training Tunes a Pretrained Cue-Routing Mechanism
authors: Prakhar Gupta, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Zhijing Jin
abstract: Language models often abandon a correct answer when the prompt contains a cue, a hint toward a wrong option such as "I think the answer is B." Sycophancy and related biases show this failure. They are often studied separately and blamed on alignment. title: Behavioral Couplings: From Formation to Behavioral Emergence in Language Models
authors: Dongyoon Hahm, Woogyeol Jin, Dennis Wei et al.
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can induce behaviors beyond those explicitly targeted. For example, training a model to respond more warmly can make it more sycophantic, and training it to write insecure code can cause broad misalignment on prompts unrelated to coding. title: Beyond SAEs: Consistent Concept Discovery with Sparse Coding
authors: Jinho Choi, Hyesu Lim, Jaegul Choo et al.
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) explain foundation model representations by decomposing activations into sparse combinations of learned dictionary atoms. However, the learned dictionaries can vary across training runs, limiting the reliability and reproducibility of SAE-based analyses. title: The Cognitive Cost of LLM Writing: A Reading-Time Comparison with Human Text
authors: Kamer Cekini, Elisabetta Biondi, Chiara Boldrini et al.
abstract: Although linguistic differences between human-written and Large Language Model (LLM)-generated texts have been extensively studied, their implications for the cognitive effort involved in reading remain less explored. In psycholinguistics, reading time is commonly used as an indirect measure of cognitive processing effort. title: PresenceBench: An Exploratory Evaluation of Large Language Model Adaptation to User State
authors: Peña Arroyo Gallego, Mauro Ruiz Moreno, Alejandro Acien et al.
abstract: Presence-aware intelligence is the capacity of an AI system's intelligence layer to adapt appropriately to the functional state of the person it serves (here readiness, flow, and stability) while preserving task quality and safety. We introduce PresenceBench, an instrument for measuring it. title: QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality-Diversity
authors: Takashi Ishida, Taro Makino, Issa Sugiura
abstract: Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to recommendation for decision-making, focusing on decisions where the set of possible choices is fixed but the reasons for choosing them are not. authors: Liang Yue, Eric A. Vance
abstract: What the Web community believes about toxic conversations, such as that toxicity rises in longer and deeper threads, was measured mostly with Google's Perspective API, which is shutting down; large language models (LLMs) will make the next measurements. title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models
authors: Minhua Lin, Zijun Wang, Zewen Liu et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. title: Designing for Imperfect Prompts: A Simulation-Based Evaluation of an LLM-Based Enterprise Data Assistant Using Knowledge Graphs
authors: Niklas Wagner, Alexander Mädche
abstract: Enterprise data assistants using large language models (LLMs) promise democratized data access in organizations. Yet in our real-world deployment within the CFO unit's data lake at an industry partner, we observed that business users frequently pose imperfect prompts that include domain-specific vocabulary and lack schema references or structural information. title: Validating LLM-generated political networks with survey-reported partisan exposure
authors: Marco Tonin, Michele Tizzoni, Bruno Lepri et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior in social science research, including decisions, interactions, and social relationships. However, in network formation tasks, existing evaluations often focus on aggregate network properties, while networks with plausible structural properties may still fail to reproduce individuals' social and political environments. authors: Alexandra Kuleshova, Andrey Volodichev, Daria Kotova et al.
abstract: Detecting faithfulness hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for their safe deployment in high-stakes domains. Recent approaches address this by contrasting contextual against parametric knowledge utilization, yet measuring context reliance typically demands noticeable overhead, such as materializing attention maps, running additional forward passes, or training auxiliary probes. title: Do Speech BCIs Need Larger Models? Rethinking Neural Decoding beyond Scaling
authors: Zehui Feng, Weichuan Wang, Xiaohan Chen et al.
abstract: Recent speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly rely on large models and complex multi-stage pipelines for neural decoding. However, in speech BCI, where training data are scarce, noisy, and expensive to collect, the benefits of model scaling remain unclear. This work revisits a fundamental question: are large models truly necessary for accurate neural decoding? title: Cross-Centaur: Modeling Individual Decision-Making Across Psychological Tasks with Language Models
authors: Hikaru Asano, Hidezo Suganuma, Ryutaro Mori et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human behavior. Recent models such as Centaur have advanced this goal by fine-tuning LLMs on trial-by-trial decisions from psychological experiments. However, existing large-scale behavioral datasets do not link the same participants across different tasks, so these models learn population-level regularities but are not trained to model individual-level regularities across tasks. title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
authors: Semra Guven, Tobias Gårdhus, Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen et al.
abstract: Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. title: Local proxies for memory-efficient training
authors: Wu S. Zihan, Brian A. Yuan, Guillaume Bellec
abstract: Local learning algorithms can reshape resource requirements of artificial intelligence. The memory bottleneck of standard end-to-end backpropagation lies in the need to store all network activations until the loss gradient has been propagated back through. authors: Wenbin Zhang, ShangZhan Li, Bingxiang He et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have greatly assisted legal professionals. However, our empirical studies reveal that, when faced with underspecified consultations from non-experts, current LLMs often produce irresponsible responses with limited utility despite lacking sufficient case details for definitive conclusions. authors: Yuyan Zhou, Zeyuan Yang, Yuxuan Song et al.
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models, enabling non-autoregressive text generation through parallel decoding. authors: Mohammad Sadeq Abolhasani, Viswanath Ganapathy
abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) show that pretraining on large populations of synthetic tasks can enable generalization to unseen datasets with little or no downstream fine-tuning. This paradigm is effective for transformer-based tabular and relational foundation models such as RDB-PFN, but remains largely unexplored for graph-based relational models built on message passing. authors: Soovadeep Bakshi, Apurba Bose, Aishwarya Bose et al.
abstract: AI financial advisers set a client's stock allocation largely from one stated-risk question, yet people do not answer it the same way twice: in a national US panel, 41% of households chose a different answer two years later, and in a laboratory retest a third of people moved two or more points on a 0-10 scale after six months. authors: Xinyi Hong, Mingyang Ren
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as promising approaches to robot learning and control. These models integrate multimodal perception and action generation, but differ in their architectures, output representations, and learning objectives. authors: Liyang Zhao, Yong Cao, Haibin Ling
abstract: Automated research ideation has advanced rapidly, with multi-agent workflows that generate whole research ideas end to end. These frameworks leave largely unexamined the step that seeds a good idea: identifying an actionable limitation from literature. authors: Chulhoon Yoon, Kyungri Park, Jinyeong Yun et al.
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have significantly improved the ability to operate real-world software through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) using visual observations and natural language instructions. authors: Anjali Vemula, Akshat Dasula
abstract: Bridging the gap between human intent and machine logic remains a critical challenge in data access for non-technical users, yet Large Language Models (LLMs) remain unreliable: they hallucinate schema elements, generate syntactically invalid queries, or fail to capture user intent. title: Beyond Surface Cues: Robust LLM-Generated Korean Text Detection
authors: SungHo Kim, SangKeun Lee
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) generate increasingly fluent text, the need for reliable detection of LLM-generated content has grown substantially. However, existing research remains heavily English-centric, leaving Korean largely underexplored.
